name: Erik Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Erik. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a tyre and exhaust chain, the branch next to the retail park roundabout. It's fast work: tyres, brakes, batteries, exhausts, a car in and out every forty minutes. I'm the junior of four fitters, three years in, and I'm still the one who gets the simple jobs while Gary, the branch manager, does the tricky diagnostics. I like it because I know what each day looks like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Sanne, who works in a bank call centre. My grandad left me his little flat when he died, so I rent that out and we live in a cheaper place, which means we've got a good bit put by. I'm not a gadget person. I don't use any of the AI stuff, my phone's four years old and I like it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every few years there's something that's going to change everything, and then tyres still need fitting. I wouldn't really go on about it, I'm not one for posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad. I'm not built for learning new screens, and in this picture I don't have to. The branch keeps running, I keep fitting tyres, and the rent from the flat keeps coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much different. I'd keep working at the branch, keep the flat rented, and maybe ask Gary to start showing me the four-wheel alignment machine, because that's the one job I can't do yet. Sanne and I would keep saving the way we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Sanne works in a bank call centre. Would AI taking routine tasks touch her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, actually, now you say it. Her job is mostly answering the same questions all day. If even the boring version of AI does some of that, her team might shrink a bit, but she's good and she'd probably be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you already worry about, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot. The chain closed two branches in the next town last year, which got people talking. Ours is busy, though, and there are plenty of garages around if it ever shut.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because tyres still need fitting whatever the hype.
I'd keep it **low-key**, since I'm not one for posting online.
think: I'd be **glad**, because I'm not built for learning new screens.
The branch keeps running and the **flat's rent** keeps coming in.
do: Keep fitting tyres at the **branch** and keep the flat rented out.
Ask the branch manager to teach him the **alignment machine**.
feel: **Calm**, because it's the world he already lives in.
S0.quote: Every few years there's something that's going to change everything, and then tyres still need fitting.
fieldNote: His cushion is solid: **rental income** from his late grandad's flat plus savings.
He only thought of his **girlfriend's call-centre job** when prompted.
The chain closing **two nearby branches** is a mild background worry.

steps.text: Keep fitting tyres and exhausts at the same chain branch
Learn the four-wheel alignment machine from the branch manager

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just how things go, every job changes. I wouldn't blame anyone in particular. If someone at the branch asked, I'd say we'll be fine, cars still need tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm less sure. Head office already books our jobs and orders stock by computer. If AI takes all that over, they'll start timing us even harder and maybe run branches with three fitters instead of four. I'm the junior, so I'd be the one to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work faster, and I'd let Gary teach me the alignment machine and the diagnostics, even though I'd hate the screen side. I'd keep the flat rented rather than selling it, because it's a safe income. I wouldn't touch the AI tools unless Gary made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's still there, but I'd notice every new thing head office sends down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one to go, but also that you'd be fine. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. The branch might lose a fitter and that might be me, but there are other garages and I've got the flat. So it's a worry, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sanne, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bigger one, honestly. Answering customers is right there in the list, and that's what my girlfriend does all day at the bank. If her team gets cut, we'd be living on my wage and the rent, which is fine, but she'd be gutted.

say: I'd say **every job changes** and I wouldn't blame anyone in particular.
I'd tell colleagues we'll be **fine** because cars still need tyres.
think: Head office could **cut a fitter**, and as the junior I'd go first.
My girlfriend's **call-centre job** is more at risk than mine.
do: Learn the **alignment machine** and diagnostics from the branch manager.
Keep the **flat rented** rather than selling it, for steady income.
Avoid **AI tools** unless the manager insists.
feel: **Uneasy**, noticing every new thing head office sends down.
S1.quote: Answering customers is right there in the list, and that's what my girlfriend does all day at the bank.
fieldNote: He says "fine" publicly but privately expects to be **first cut** as the junior.
His **girlfriend's job** worries him more than his own.
Resists AI tools and would only use them **under instruction**.

steps.text: Learn alignment and diagnostics from the branch manager this year
Keep fitting tyres and working faster at the branch
Keep the grandad's flat rented out as steady income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the government should slow it down somehow, even if I don't know how. I'm usually in the middle on things, but two years is ridiculous. I'd still not post about it, I'd just say it at the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think our branch goes early. Tyre fitting is the most repetitive job in the trade, the kind of thing robots will do first once they arrive in 2031. Before that, head office would run everything with AI and cut staff. I'd be thirty with no other skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending on the car and holidays straight away. I'd keep the flat, because rent is the one thing that doesn't depend on my job, maybe even raise it a bit. I'd ask around about jobs that need a person, like a council depot or road crew, though I'd put it off as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. I don't do well with things changing, and this is everything changing at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. I've got a nice one on finance and I'd sell it and get something old. Then the holiday we booked for next summer. I'd keep enough for Sanne and me to live on two years if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, probably. He worked at the same printing works for thirty years until it closed, and he went into driving buses. He'd say just get on with it, which is annoying but usually right.

say: I'd say **two years is ridiculous** and the government should slow it down.
I'd only say it **at the branch**, not online.
think: Tyre fitting is the **most repetitive** job, so robots take it first in 2031.
I'd be **thirty** with **no other skills** when it goes.
do: Sell the **financed car** and cancel next summer's holiday.
Keep the **flat rented** and raise the rent a little.
Ask about **council depot** or road crew jobs, though slowly.
S2.quote: Tyre fitting is the most repetitive job in the trade, the kind of thing robots will do first once they arrive in 2031.
fieldNote: His **centre outlook** bends here: he wants government to slow it down.
Rent from the **inherited flat** is the anchor of his whole plan.
His dad's **printing-works closure** is his only model for starting over.

steps.text: Sell the financed car and cancel next summer's holiday
Keep the inherited flat rented and raise the rent slightly
Ask about council depot and road crew jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fast but people can cope. At work I'd probably say we'll see, let's not panic. I'd let other people do the shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd give myself until about 2033. AGI in 2031 takes the booking and stock side, then robots around 2034 take the fitting. That's seven years. I'd be thirty-four, which is still young, but I'm not quick at picking up new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the branch for most of it and save harder, an extra three hundred a month. I'd ask my dad to put a word in at the bus depot for around 2032, because driving is something I know. And I'd keep the flat, obviously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the two-year one, but it'd sit there under everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning the AI tools, given the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd rather move to something hands-on than learn screens at thirty, and I know that might be the wrong call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think buses will still need drivers by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe not for long. But a bus driver at least has passengers to look after, and people might want a person there for a while longer.

say: I'd say **five years** is fast, but people can cope.
At work I'd say **let's not panic** and leave the shouting to others.
think: I'd give myself until **about 2033** before fitting goes in 2034.
At thirty-four I'm **still young**, but slow at new things.
do: Save an **extra three hundred** a month from wages.
Ask his dad about **bus driving** jobs around 2032.
feel: **Anxious**, sitting under everything, though less than the two-year picture.
S3.quote: I'd rather move to something hands-on than learn screens at thirty, and I know that might be the wrong call.
fieldNote: Openly admits his refusal to learn AI **might be wrong**, but sticks to it.
Plans a **bus-driving move** through his dad's contacts.
Honest that he **doesn't know** whether buses will keep drivers.

steps.text: Save an extra three hundred a month
Ask his dad to put a word in at the bus depot
Keep working at the tyre branch until about 2033

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most of us will sort ourselves out. I'd probably be the one at the break table telling people to stop worrying. Same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years plus three for robots takes me to forty. I'd still need to change at some point, which I don't like. But I can put that off for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at the branch, learn the alignment and maybe the diagnostics. Around 2034 I'd start looking for something else, maybe a council job. Sanne and I would probably buy a house in the next couple of years using the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. It's a long way off, but I know myself, I'll leave it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'll leave it too late. What would stop that happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sanne, probably. She makes the plans in our house. If she put a date on the fridge, I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the flat at any point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's the one thing my grandad left me and it pays. If everything else goes, my grandad's flat is still there, and it pays.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and most people will sort themselves out.
I'd be the one at the **break table** telling people to stop worrying.
think: Ten years plus three takes me to **forty** before robots arrive.
I'll still need to **change** eventually, which I don't like.
do: Learn **alignment** and maybe diagnostics at the branch.
Buy a **house** with his girlfriend in the next couple of years.
feel: A bit **anxious**, knowing he tends to leave things too late.
S4.quote: If everything else goes, my grandad's flat is still there, and it pays.
fieldNote: Even with a decade he stays **anxious** because he knows he delays change.
Relies on his **girlfriend** to set deadlines for him.
The **inherited flat** is emotional security as well as money.

steps.text: Keep working at the tyre branch and learn the alignment machine
Start looking for a council job around 2034
Buy a house with his girlfriend in the next two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is someone telling me clearly which jobs will still be around, and a way into them that doesn't need a load of screens. I'm good with my hands, I just need a door to walk through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe that people like me don't really go looking for help. Someone would have to come and find us at the branch.

headlineQuote: I'm good with my hands, I just need a door to walk through.
portrait: Erik is the **junior fitter** at a tyre and exhaust chain branch, three years in.
He lives with his girlfriend, who works in a **bank call centre**, and rents out his late grandad's flat.
He **avoids AI tools** and prefers predictable, hands-on routine.
His mood slides from **calm** to alarmed as AGI speeds up, peaking at two years.
He blames nobody in particular but wants **government to slow** the fastest picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because repetitive tyre work goes first and he has no other skills.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear information** about which jobs will last.
A **hands-on route** into new work that doesn't rely on screens.
